vecchio: For the CPU pipeline, threading was maximised by setting `OMP_NUM_THREADS`, `MKL_NUM_THREADS`, `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS`, and `NUMBA_NUM_THREADS` to 100 (the usable core count) before importing any numerical library. These variables target the thread pools of four distinct parallel backends that NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, and UMAP may dispatch to: OpenMP (used by OpenBLAS and several `sklearn` inner loops), Intel MKL, OpenBLAS, and Numba (the JIT backend of `umap-learn`). Only the pool corresponding to the BLAS library that NumPy was linked against at build time is actually active at runtime; the other variables are harmlessly ignored. We set all four to remain portable across container variants where the BLAS choice may differ; in our RAPIDS base image, NumPy is linked against OpenBLAS.
nuovo: For the CPU pipeline, `OMP_NUM_THREADS`, `MKL_NUM_THREADS`, `OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS` and `NUMBA_NUM_THREADS` were set to 100, the number of CPUs (hardware threads) allocated by SLURM, before any numerical library was imported, so that the OpenMP, BLAS and Numba thread pools used by NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and umap-learn were all sized to the allocation. Neighbour search was the exception: from 8,192 cells upward, that is at every benchmark size, Scanpy 1.12 builds the k-NN graph with pynndescent and passes it the Scanpy default `n_jobs` = 1, so Numba ran on one thread during this step. In a separate measurement on the spatial GPU workstation (PCA embeddings recomputed from the 10,000-, 50,000- and 100,000-cell benchmark files; five repeats per setting, one process each, timing the call after JIT compilation), `n_jobs` = 100 made this step 1.16, 1.91 and 2.48 times faster than `n_jobs` = 1.

nuovo: ### Multi-GPU configuration

vecchio: For datasets exceeding single-GPU VRAM capacity (500k and 1.3M cells), we employed a hybrid multi-GPU pipeline using Dask-CUDA [@Rocklin2015].
nuovo: At every dataset size we also ran a hybrid configuration with a Dask [@Rocklin2015] and Dask-CUDA [@RAPIDS2024] cluster of 2, 4 or 8 workers, one per GPU, each with a 10 GB initial / 70 GB maximum RMM pool. Data loading, QC, normalisation and HVG selection ran in Scanpy on the host CPU, and the HVG-subset matrix was then transferred to GPU 0 as a CuPy array. Because it was not converted to a Dask array, scaling, PCA, neighbour search, Leiden, UMAP and DE all ran on GPU 0, and the additional GPUs did not take part in the computation; rapids-singlecell 0.14.1 provides Dask-based routes for QC metrics, total-count normalisation, scaling and PCA, among other steps, which this configuration did not use. The 8-GPU runs ran on a different node from the 1-, 2- and 4-GPU runs (Section "Hardware and software environment"). Results at 500k and 1.3M cells come only from this configuration, because the single-GPU pipeline failed during QC at these sizes (at 500k cells an allocation of 23.8 GiB exceeded the RMM pool, whose maximum is the whole device memory; at 1.3M cells QC stopped with a CUDA illegal-memory-access error).

vecchio: In this hybrid pipeline, data loading, QC, normalisation, HVG selection and scaling executed on the host CPU. This reflects the structure of the available software rather than a design preference: at 500k and 1.3M cells the standard single-GPU pipeline exceeded the 80 GB VRAM of a single H100 (Table 4), so the Dask-CUDA path was the only way to run these dataset sizes at all, and within that path only PCA and neighbour graph construction had distributed GPU implementations usable for the pipeline as configured here. The constraint is therefore one of the current software stack, not a property of the operations themselves: on a single GPU, normalisation is 329x faster than CPU (Fig. 1), and distributing preprocessing across GPUs is precisely the direction we identify for future frameworks (see Discussion).

vecchio: To determine the maximum dataset size processable on a single DGX H100 node, we implemented a memory-optimised pipeline variant.
nuovo: To determine the maximum dataset size processable on a single DGX H100 node, we implemented a memory-optimised pipeline variant. The stress test used the 3,436,470-cell Census selection described above (and random subsets of it at 1.7M and 3.4M cells, seed = 42). Larger sizes were built by concatenating whole copies of the dataset, with renamed cell identifiers, plus a random draw of the remaining cells (6.9M cells: 2 copies; 10.3M: 3 copies; 11.9M: 3 copies plus 1,590,590 cells), so duplicated cells are present in the expression matrix and in the k-NN graph. Because duplicated cells reach the `min_cells` = 3 threshold, the number of genes passing QC grew with replication (41,344 at 3.44M, 42,394 at 6.87M and 44,158 from 10.3M cells). At 3,436,470, 6,872,940 and 10,309,410 cells, cuML KMeans with k = 50, 100 and 200 replaced the three Leiden resolutions. DE was skipped (`--skip-de`) at every size except 1.7M and 3.4M cells.

vecchio: The key optimisations were: (i) scaling on CPU rather than GPU (leveraging 2 TB system RAM); (ii) a distributed covariance PCA that scatters the scaled matrix across all 8 GPUs, computes per-GPU partial covariance matrices (each 2,000 x 2,000), sums and eigendecomposes on GPU 0, then projects locally, which is mathematically equivalent to standard PCA via the covariance method; (iii) lean GPU transfer that replaces the dense matrix with an empty sparse placeholder after PCA, since downstream steps (neighbours, clustering, UMAP) only require the PCA embedding; and (iv) a reduced RMM pool (2 GB per worker).
nuovo: The key optimisations were: (i) scaling on CPU rather than GPU (leveraging 2 TB system RAM); (ii) a covariance PCA in which the parent process scattered the scaled matrix across the 8 GPUs, computed per-GPU partial products (2,000 x 2,000), summed and eigendecomposed them on GPU 0 and projected locally; the matrix was not re-centred after clipping at `max_value` = 10 and partial products were accumulated in float32, so the result approximates, but is not identical to, standard PCA; (iii) lean GPU transfer that replaces the dense matrix with an empty sparse placeholder after PCA, since downstream steps (neighbours, clustering, UMAP) only require the PCA embedding; and (iv) a reduced RMM pool (2 GB) for each Dask-CUDA worker; the workers were started but performed no computation.

vecchio: We conducted a binary search from 3.4M to 13.7M cells to identify the failure point. CPU memory was recorded as the resident set size of the parent Python process (`psutil.Process().memory_info().rss`), sampled immediately before and after each pipeline step and preceded by an explicit garbage collection; the reported peak is the maximum over these post-step samples. This instrumentation yields a lower bound on the job's true memory use for two reasons: it cannot observe allocations that are made and released within a single step, and it excludes the resident memory of the eight Dask-CUDA worker processes, which the SLURM cgroup does account for.
nuovo: We ran the memory-optimised pipeline at 15 sizes from 3.4M to 11.9M cells, refining the step size towards the failure point; single attempts at 12.0M and 13.7M cells (4 copies of the dataset) did not complete. Two further variants were run: a sparse-scatter variant computes per-gene mean and standard deviation from the sparse matrix on CPU and lets each GPU densify and scale its own chunk, so the dense matrix never exists on CPU; a chunked variant selects HVGs from per-gene statistics accumulated over 100,000-cell batches and computes PCA by batch-wise covariance accumulation. CPU memory was recorded as the resident set size of the parent Python process (`psutil.Process().memory_info().rss`), sampled immediately before and after each pipeline step, with an explicit garbage collection before each pre-step sample; the reported peak is the maximum over these post-step samples. This instrumentation yields a lower bound on the job's true memory use for two reasons: it cannot observe allocations that are made and released within a single step, and it excludes the resident memory of the eight Dask-CUDA worker processes, which the SLURM cgroup does account for. The replication of the dataset for sizes above 3,436,470 cells ran between data loading and QC, outside any timed step: at 11.9M cells it accounts for the 302.34 GiB increase between these two samples, and its transient peak was not sampled. GPU memory was recorded with NVML as device memory in use, summed over the eight GPUs; it includes the RMM pools of the Dask-CUDA workers. All memory values are in GiB (bytes / 1024^3).

vecchio: Differential expression testing at atlas scale is constrained by hardware, which shaped the factorial design of this benchmark. At 3.4 million cells and 41,000 genes the raw count matrix (`adata.raw.X`) occupies approximately 121 GB in sparse CSR format, exceeding the 80 GB VRAM of any single H100 device; running GPU DE naively is therefore impossible, and the tests we benchmark either scatter genes across multiple GPUs or stream gene chunks through a single GPU. We evaluated seven DE strategies in a factorial design crossing test type (Wilcoxon, t-test, pseudo-bulk) with GPU strategy (none, scatter-by-genes across 8 GPUs, chunk-and-stream on 1 GPU). Gene chunks of 500 were used for GPU strategies, giving 500 x 3.4M x 4 bytes approximately 6.8 GB per chunk, well within the 80 GB per-device limit. Pseudo-bulk aggregation summed raw counts by donor x cluster, normalised to counts per million, log-transformed, and applied the Wilcoxon test on the aggregated matrix [@Squair2021].
nuovo: DE was benchmarked on a 3,400,000-cell random subset of the Census selection (seed = 42; 3,399,892 cells and 41,321 genes in `adata.raw` after QC). Differential expression testing at atlas scale is constrained by hardware, which shaped the design of this benchmark. The matrix used for DE, `adata.raw.X`, holds log-normalised values rather than raw counts in this pipeline, and the GPU tests processed it in gene chunks, either scattered across GPUs or streamed through a single GPU. We timed six DE configurations (Table 7): a t-test on CPU (Scanpy); a t-test and a Wilcoxon test with gene chunks scattered across 8 GPUs; the same two tests with gene chunks streamed through one GPU; and pseudo-bulk aggregation followed by a Wilcoxon test on CPU. A Wilcoxon test on CPU was not run at this size and pseudo-bulk was not run on GPU, so the design is not a full factorial. In the scatter strategy a single host thread processed the chunks in sequence, alternating devices, so the GPUs did not work concurrently. Gene chunks of 500 were used for GPU strategies, giving 500 x 3.4M x 4 bytes approximately 6.8 GB per chunk, well within the 80 GB per-device limit. The GPU tests were custom CuPy kernels, not `rank_genes_groups`: the Wilcoxon kernel assigned ordinal ranks without averaging ties and computed neither p-values nor a multiple-testing correction, so it yields a rank-sum statistic used here for timing only. GPU timings start after `adata.raw.X` was converted to CSC format, whereas CPU timings cover the whole `rank_genes_groups` call. Pseudo-bulk aggregation summed the values of `adata.raw.X` over donor x cluster groups (Census `donor_id`, 202 donors; groups with fewer than 5 cells discarded; 2,431 pseudo-samples over 81 clusters), re-normalised the sums to counts per million, applied a second log transformation and compared clusters with a Wilcoxon test. We use this aggregation as a timing proxy for pseudo-bulk analysis; count-based methods such as edgeR or DESeq2 are recommended for pseudo-bulk DE between conditions [@Squair2021].

vecchio: Spatial benchmarks used two 10x Genomics public datasets, both downloaded programmatically from the 10x Genomics public data portal. The first is Visium v1 Mouse Brain Sagittal Anterior, the standard spot-based spatial transcriptomics platform, consisting of 2,695 spots at 55 um resolution and approximately 32,285 genes. The second is Visium HD Mouse Brain (CytAssist, FFPE), benchmarked at two bin sizes: 8 um (393,543 bins) and 2 um (subsampled from the native 6.3 million down to 389,492 bins), each quantifying 19,059 genes. The Visium HD 2 um dataset was subsampled to approximately 400,000 bins using the `--max-spots` flag so that the benchmark would fit within the RTX 4090's 24 GB VRAM; full-scale analysis of the complete 6.3 million bins requires DGX-class resources.
nuovo: Spatial benchmarks used two 10x Genomics public datasets, both obtained from the 10x Genomics public data portal. The first is Visium v1 Mouse Brain Sagittal Anterior, the standard spot-based spatial transcriptomics platform, consisting of 2,695 spots at 55 um resolution and approximately 32,285 genes. The second is the Visium HD Spatial Gene Expression Library, Mouse Brain (FFPE), processed by 10x Genomics with Space Ranger 3.0.0 (CytAssist; Visium Mouse Transcriptome Probe Set v2.0), benchmarked at two bin sizes: 8 um (393,543 bins) and 2 um (6,296,688 bins, randomly subsampled to 400,000 bins with seed 42; 389,492 after QC), each quantifying 19,059 genes. The Visium HD 2 um dataset was subsampled to 400,000 bins using the `--max-spots` flag so that the benchmark would fit within the RTX 4090's 24 GB VRAM. Random subsampling kept 6.35% of the 2 um bins, so the subsample has the bin density of a regular grid with a spacing of about 8 um, and its spatial neighbour graph and autocorrelation statistics do not describe the native 2 um resolution.

vecchio: We note that GPU floating-point arithmetic is non-deterministic due to non-associative parallel reductions [@Shanmugavelu2024; @Collange2015], and quantify the resulting divergence through the concordance metrics above rather than expecting bit-identical outputs.
nuovo: GPU reductions that use atomic operations can make results vary between runs because floating-point addition is not associative [@Collange2015; @Shanmugavelu2024]. In our runs GPU Leiden labels were identical across the five repeats at 10,000 cells in every GPU configuration, but differed between repeats in every configuration from 100,000 cells upward (and in three of the four at 50,000 cells), whereas CPU labels were identical across repeats at every size. CPU-GPU differences also arise from different algorithms and settings (Leiden implementation and iterations, PCA solver, neighbour search), which the concordance metrics capture together with numerical effects.

Testi estratti di Collange2015 e Shanmugavelu2024 (pacchetto revisione) letti: non associatività e riduzioni con atomicAdd su GPU.
